title: Salesforce Wrike Integration in 2026, Set Up Without Code
summary: Salesforce Wrike integration automates work creation when records change. The fastest approach uses visual automation platforms or direct code integration.
body_markdown:
## Fix Salesforce Wrike workflow failures


When a Salesforce Wrike workflow breaks, **it is usually one of six failures** : an expired connection, a rate limit, missing API access in your edition, Wrike permissions, mismatched fields, and duplicate tasks.


Each has a fix. These were checked against the vendors' own documentation on 2026-11-21.


### Salesforce Wrike connection and permission errors


When a run fails with` INVALID_SESSION_ID` or a 401, the workflow is still running but its login has stopped working. That usually happens after a password change, a revoked token, or a deactivated user.


Reconnect the account in your automation tool, using a dedicated integration user rather than a person, so one employee leaving doesn't silently stop your handoffs.


On the Wrike side, it fails differently. The connection is valid, but the task isn't created, because the connected user can't see the target folder or project.


Open that folder as the integration user. If you can't add a task by hand, the workflow can't either. Grant that user access, then re-run the failed record.


### API limits and edition requirements


When Salesforce returns` REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` , or Wrike a 429, you asked too often. Each platform caps how many API calls an account can make in a period, and a workflow that checks for changes on a timer spends that allowance even when nothing changed.


Switch to an event trigger so a call happens only when a record changes. Add a delay and retry for bursts, such as a bulk import creating hundreds of tasks at once, since bulk imports can trigger rate limiting.


Quieter still is edition access. Salesforce API access depends on which edition you bought, and some editions need an add-on. If a connection authenticates but returns nothing useful, your edition may not include API access.


Ask your Salesforce administrator to confirm API access against the current documentation before you blame the workflow. Check your Wrike plan the same way if an action you need is missing.


### Field mapping and duplicate records


When the value Salesforce sends isn't one Wrike accepts, that's a field mismatch. Typical causes are a dropdown value that doesn't exist on the other side, a date in the wrong format, or an empty required field.


Test with a real record that has awkward data, such as a blank field or an unusual status. Then map to values that exist in both systems.


If you see duplicate tasks, the cause is a trigger that fires on every edit, or a retry that re-creates a task the first attempt already made.


Save the Wrike task ID back on the Salesforce record. Before creating anything, check whether that field is already filled. Narrow the trigger to the one change that matters, such as a stage moving to Closed Won.


When something still goes wrong, open the run history. It shows which step failed and what data it received.
